title: Max Consecutive Ones: count longest run of 1s.
shortTitle: Max Consecutive Ones: Longest Run of 1s
keyPoints: Single-pass linear scan with two counters: current streak and best streak seen so far
On each 1, increment current and update best; on each 0, reset current to zero
Update best on every 1 to avoid the end-of-array special case
The generalization to flipping at most K zeros is a sliding window (Max Consecutive Ones III)
O(n) time and O(1) space with no extra data structures
An empty array yields zero naturally because the loop never runs

s1_definition.oneliner: Count the current run of ones, update the best, and reset the current run to zero on every zero.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Max Consecutive Ones** – find the length of the longest unbroken run of the value 1 in a binary array.
- **Two counters** – a current counter tracks the active streak of ones; a best counter remembers the longest streak seen.
- **On each 1** – increment the current counter and update best if current exceeds it.
- **On each 0** – reset the current counter to zero because the streak is broken.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space, single pass with no extra data structures.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India records whether each day had a successful end-of-day settlement for Rajesh's account: 1 for success, 0 for failure. Operations wants the longest streak of consecutive successful days as a reliability metric. A clerk walks through the days once, counting how many successes in a row right now, and whenever that current streak beats the best streak, the best is updated. A single failed day resets the current streak to zero.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Max Consecutive Ones finds the longest unbroken run of 1s in a binary array with a single pass and two counters. A current counter measures the run of ones ending at the position you are looking at, and a best counter remembers the longest run seen. On each 1 you increment the current counter and update the best. On each 0 you reset the current counter to zero because the streak is broken.

The small but real detail is to update best on every 1 rather than only on zeros. Updating only on zeros requires a post-loop fix to catch a trailing run of ones that never hits a zero, which is easy to forget. Updating on every 1 avoids that edge case entirely.

The natural extension is the version where you may flip at most K zeros to ones, which is a sliding window problem: grow the right edge, count zeros, and shrink the left edge when the zero count exceeds K. The plain problem is the K=0 case, and recognizing that connection shows the interviewer you understand the general pattern.

In the operations team at the National Bank of India, Rajesh's daily settlement history is a binary array, and the team reports the longest streak of consecutive successful days as a reliability metric. The single-pass count-and-reset approach handles years of daily data in constant memory, and the sliding-window generalization answers management's what-if about allowing a small number of excused failures.

Remember one sentence: count the current run, update the best on every 1, and reset on every 0.
